content: 1. Norgestrel and Ethinyl Estradiol are oral contraceptive agents approved by the FDA for the prevention of pregnancy in women who choose to use this method of contraception. 2. WikiDoc does not guarantee the validity of its content and is not a substitute for professional healthcare providers. It is intended solely as an educational tool and not for healthcare delivery. 3. The educational content on WikiDoc drug pages is based on FDA package inserts, National Library of Medicine content, and established practice guidelines or consensus statements. 4. WikiDoc does not endorse the use of any medication or device in a manner inconsistent with its labeling. 5. Norgestrel and Ethinyl Estradiol carry a Black Box Warning, indicating significant risks associated with their use. 6. Common adverse reactions to these oral contraceptives include weight changes, abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, muscle cramps, headaches, mood swings, amenorrhea, breakthrough bleeding, breast tenderness, nipple discharge, menstrual disorders, breast pain, and scanty vaginal bleeding. 7. For maximum contraceptive effectiveness, oral contraceptives must be taken exactly as directed, at intervals not exceeding 24 hours. 8. A 28-day dosing schedule involves taking one white tablet daily for 21 days, followed by one peach tablet daily for 7 days, regardless of whether bleeding has stopped. 9. Women should use an additional method of contraception during the first 7 days of the initial cycle of oral contraceptive use. 10. Due to the increased risk of thromboembolism postpartum, oral contraceptives should not be initiated earlier than 4-6 weeks after a full-term delivery. 11. If pregnancy is terminated within the first 12 weeks, oral contraceptives should be started immediately or within 7 days. If terminated after 12 weeks, they should be started after 2 weeks. 12. If spotting or breakthrough bleeding occurs, the patient should continue the medication as scheduled. Persistent bleeding should prompt consultation with a physician. 13. If a single pill is missed, it should be taken as soon as remembered, and the next pill should be taken at the regular time. Missing a pill may cause spotting or light bleeding. 14. If more than one pill is missed, detailed patient instructions should be followed regarding how to proceed. 15. If a menstrual period is missed and the prescribed dosage regimen was not followed, pregnancy should be considered, and oral contraceptives should be withheld until pregnancy is ruled out. 16. Oral contraceptives are contraindicated in women with conditions such as thromboembolic disorders, a history of deep vein thrombosis, cerebrovascular or coronary artery disease, known or suspected breast or estrogen-dependent cancers, undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, liver tumors, or known or suspected pregnancy. 17. The use of oral contraceptives is associated with increased risks of myocardial infarction, thromboembolism, stroke, hepatic neoplasia, and gallbladder disease, particularly in women with underlying risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and diabetes. 18. Smoking significantly increases the risk of myocardial infarction in women using oral contraceptives, especially those over 35 years of age. 19. Oral contraceptives may exacerbate risk factors for cardiovascular disease, such as hypertension, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. They should be used cautiously in women with these conditions. 20. An increased risk of thromboembolic and thrombotic diseases, including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, is well-established with oral contraceptive use. 21. Oral contraceptives should be discontinued at least 4 weeks prior to and for 2 weeks after elective surgery or during prolonged immobilization to reduce the risk of thromboembolism. 22. Oral contraceptives should not be started earlier than 4-6 weeks postpartum in women who are not breastfeeding, due to the increased risk of thromboembolism. 23. An increased risk of cerebrovascular events, including thrombotic and hemorrhagic strokes, has been observed in oral contraceptive users, particularly in older hypertensive women who smoke. 24. A positive association exists between the dose of estrogen and progestogen in oral contraceptives and the risk of vascular disease. Lower-dose formulations are associated with reduced risks. 25. Persistent risk of vascular disease has been observed in some studies even after discontinuation of oral contraceptives, particularly in older women with prolonged use. 26. Epidemiological studies suggest no significant increase in the risk of breast cancer with oral contraceptive use, although some studies report a slight increase in risk, particularly with long-term use. 27. Oral contraceptives have been associated with an increased risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in some populations, but the extent to which this is due to other factors remains controversial. 28. Benign hepatic adenomas are associated with oral contraceptive use, although the incidence is rare. Long-term use may increase the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, but these cancers are extremely rare. 29. Retinal thrombosis has been reported with oral contraceptive use. Unexplained vision loss or other ocular symptoms should prompt immediate discontinuation and evaluation. 30. Extensive studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who used oral contraceptives prior to pregnancy or inadvertently during early pregnancy. 31. Oral contraceptives should not be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. 32. Oral contraceptives may cause glucose intolerance and hyperinsulinism, particularly with higher estrogen doses. Diabetic and prediabetic women should be monitored closely. 33. Women with a history of hypertension should consider alternative methods of contraception. 34. Breakthrough bleeding and spotting are common during the first three months of oral contraceptive use. Persistent or recurrent abnormal bleeding should be evaluated to rule out malignancy or pregnancy. 35. Oral contraceptives do not protect against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. Women should be counseled accordingly. 36.
